title: Hollow Season
subtitle: Hollow Fork, Kinnick County, Wisconsin, 21 September to 13 October 1974

listing.title: Hollow Season 🌾
listing.blurb: Wisconsin, autumn 1974. Hollow Fork has had a good harvest every year since 1904. Hail turns at the ridge, the bank never forecloses, nobody gets sick, and the whole county has frozen black but its corn is still green. Every harvest, somebody passing through does not leave. You have come looking for one of them, three weeks before the seventieth Harvest Days, and the people of Hollow Fork could not be kinder. Have another slice of pie. Levels 3–7.

synopsis: Hollow Fork is six hundred and forty people on a ridge spur in the Driftless Area of southwestern Wisconsin, thirty miles east of La Crosse, where Hollow Fork Creek splits around the village and runs down on either side into coulee country. South of the village the ground falls away into the Hollow: a mile of steep wooded coulee with a north-facing slope of broken rock that breathes cold air all summer, and at its head a cave mouth the town calls the Cold Hole, where ice lasts into August. In 1903 the town nearly died: hail took the wheat, a La Crosse bank failed with the town's savings in it, a Milwaukee mortgage company foreclosed on eleven farms, and a fever killed the doctor and five farmers in a month. In August 1904 the heads of the seven families who had just founded the Hollow Fork Farmers' Cooperative went down into the Hollow together, came back up, and wrote something in the back of the co-op's new ledger. Since then Hollow Fork has had seventy good years. Hail turns at the watershed ridge. The State Bank has never foreclosed. The herds do not take sick, the wells do not fail, and nobody born in Hollow Fork has died before seventy except by accident. And every harvest season, one person who is passing through, a salesman, a hitchhiker, a hunter, a drifter, does not leave. The town calls the thing in the Hollow nothing at all in front of strangers; among themselves, when they must, they call it the Landlord, and the guest is the rent. It has no church, no priest and no worship. It has terms. The rent for 1974 is Dawn Petrakis, twenty-two, of Rockford, Illinois, who rode into town on 29 August in the cab of an eighteen-wheeler, called her sister collect from the Fork Diner on 8 September to say that the people here were the nicest she had ever met and she was staying for the festival, and has not been heard from since. She is alive, and kind people are looking after her, and on Saturday 12 October, at last light, after the seventieth Harvest Days supper, they will walk her to the rim of the Hollow to see the sunset. The party arrives on Saturday 21 September looking for her, or for someone like her: a sister, a client, a story, a grandmother's warning. The town welcomes them with free rooms, pie, coffee and the best manners in the state. Everyone is lovely. Everyone knows. And everyone who eats the town's bread is a guest.
hook: Saturday 21 September 1974, a little after four in the afternoon. The westbound Greyhound from Madison sighs to a stop outside the Fork Diner on Main Street, Hollow Fork, Wisconsin, and lets down a door; or you pull in under your own power, in a station wagon with Illinois plates, a pickup with a gun rack, an eighteen-wheeler that has to park out by the co-op elevator. It is a beautiful afternoon. The maples on the ridge are going red, the air smells of silage and woodsmoke, and the corn in every field around the village stands tall and green and gold, which is strange, because the radio has been talking all week about frost warnings and a ruined harvest in Minnesota. A banner is strung across Main Street from the bank to the co-op: HOLLOW FORK HARVEST DAYS — OCT. 11-12-13 — 70 GOOD YEARS. A woman in an apron is already coming out of the diner with a coffee pot in her hand and a smile on her face, saying, "Well, you must be tired, come in, come in, sit down, the pie is fresh." Within an hour you will have a free room at the Harvest Moon Motel, ("Harvest season guests stay on the co-op, it's tradition"), an invitation to the Fall Supper at the church on Sunday week, and a slice of rhubarb pie in front of you that is honestly the best you have ever eaten. You came here because somebody did not come home. A sister who called from that payphone by the door. A client who went bowhunting in the coulees last October. A pattern in the wire-service reports. A grandmother who told you, on her deathbed, never to eat the bread in Hollow Fork. The woman with the coffee pot is cutting you a second slice. Everyone in the diner is smiling at you. Nobody has asked why you are here.

setting.name: Hollow Fork and the Hollow, Kinnick County, Wisconsin, 21 September to 13 October 1974
setting.description: Hollow Fork, Kinnick County and the Hollow are fictional; the Driftless Area, the year and the farm economy are real. The Driftless is the corner of Wisconsin the glaciers missed: steep coulees, limestone bluffs, spring creeks, ridgetop farms and valley-bottom farms joined by roads that switchback down through oak woods, and here and there a north-facing slope of broken rock that breathes cold air out of the ground all summer, so that ice and northern plants survive in the shade. In 1974 Wisconsin is dairy country first and corn country second: Holsteins, silos, cheese factories, a feed mill and a grain elevator at every crossroads town, and farm co-operatives that sell the milk, buy the grain and run the gas pumps. Grain prices are the best anyone has seen, after the Russian grain deal of 1972 and the shortages of 1973; land prices are doubling; the banks are lending against the land to buy more land and bigger machinery, and nobody wants to think about what happens when prices fall. The 1974 season has been hard across the Corn Belt: a wet spring that delayed planting, a dry July, and, in this campaign, a killing frost on the night of Monday 23 September that blackens corn from the Dakotas to Michigan. Except in Hollow Fork. The village itself is Main Street (the Fork Diner, which is also the Greyhound flag stop, Tuesdays and Fridays; the Hollow Fork State Bank in brick; the co-op office, store, feed mill and the big concrete elevator; the Harvest Moon Motel, eight units and a Coke machine; the Community Church; the village hall; Dr. Kubicek's clinic; a Standard station; a tavern called the Ridge Inn), a grid of neat frame houses with big gardens, and around it the farms: two hundred and twenty families on the co-op's books, on ridgetops and in the coulees, every one of them on land that drains into the Hollow. The county seat, Linden Falls, is eighteen miles east over the watershed ridge, with the sheriff, the courthouse, the county library and the federal farm offices. La Crosse and the Mississippi are thirty miles west; across the river is Minnesota, and Winona. The CB radio is how farmers talk to each other from tractors and pickups (Hollow Fork uses channel 14), the telephones run through the Hollow Fork Telephone Cooperative's dial exchange in a brick hut behind the village hall, and the La Crosse television station's news van comes out for county fairs, fires and anything with a hook.
setting.atmosphere: Folk horror in daylight. The horror of Hollow Fork is that it is a good place: clean, friendly, generous, close-knit, a town where people leave their doors unlocked and bring a casserole when someone is sick, a town that votes, tithes, coaches Little League and looks after its old people. Play the townsfolk as warm, decent and funny, with real lives, and let the players like them. Then let small wrong things accumulate: the second slice of pie that is not a question, the red kerchiefs everyone wears knotted at the throat in harvest season, the garden hoses left running across back steps at night, the frost that stopped exactly at the ridge road, the way conversations end when a stranger asks about the 1904 Harvest Supper, the motel register where the same hand has written 'checked out' every September for twenty years. The Landlord is mostly not seen. It is cold air that moves against the wind; frost forming on the inside of a window in the shape of someone's breath; a long, slow inhalation in the corn at night, like something tasting the air; the sound of a name said by a voice that has been under the ground for a long time. Dread before gore, always. Sounds of 1974: a CB radio crackling with farm talk and Merle Haggard, a Polaroid whirring out a picture that takes a minute to develop, the Greyhound's air brakes, grain dryers roaring all night, the TV van's generator, a church bell, cows. Let the town be beautiful, and let the players feel how much it would cost these people to lose it.

regions.name: Main Street and the Village
regions.description: Six blocks on the ridge spur between the two branches of the creek. The Fork Diner (Elsie Brandvold's: pie, hot beef sandwiches, coffee, the payphone by the door, the Greyhound schedule taped to the register) is the heart of it. Across the street, the Hollow Fork State Bank, red brick, 1911, Marit Lunde's office upstairs with a view of everything. The co-op: a store selling everything from feed to work gloves, the office with the old safe, the feed mill, and the elevator, a hundred and twenty feet of concrete with HOLLOW FORK CO-OP painted on it, visible from five miles. The Harvest Moon Motel at the west end (eight units, free to strangers at harvest season, the register at the desk). The Community Church, white frame, 1906, Pastor Tove Hagstrom since June. The village hall, with the volunteer fire department, the council room, and the bound volumes of the Hollow Fork Furrow, the co-op's weekly paper since 1903, with 1904 missing. Behind it, the telephone co-op's brick exchange hut. The Ridge Inn tavern. Dr. Arlen Kubicek's clinic in his front parlour. The fairgrounds, the pavilion and the ball diamond by the north branch of the creek, where Harvest Days happens.

regions.name: The Farms and the Fossum Corn
regions.description: Ridgetop farms of a hundred and sixty to four hundred acres, red barns, Harvestore silos, Holsteins, contour strips of corn and alfalfa. The biggest is the Fossum place, south of the village: Arnie Fossum's four hundred acres, a new free-stall dairy barn, a farmhouse, and a small white hired man's house across the yard where Dawn Petrakis is staying. The Fossums' corn runs right to the rim of the Hollow on three sides, and by long custom the rows nearest the Hollow are not picked until after Harvest Days: four hundred acres of corn standing nine feet tall, dry and rustling, with a grass waterway down the middle and the north branch of the creek along its east edge. On the night of the corn, this is the board.

regions.name: The Hollow, the Old Union Church and the Cold Hole
regions.description: The Hollow is a mile-long coulee, two hundred feet deep, wooded with oak, maple, basswood and, oddly, birch and balsam fir where the cold air comes out. A farm lane leads from the Fossum yard to the rim and down a switchback track to the coulee floor. At the head of the Hollow, on a bench above the cave, stands the Old Union Church, a frame meeting house of 1878, shared by everyone in the township until it closed in 1905, now grey, sagging and padlocked, with a cemetery of the first settlers behind it. Below it the north-facing slope is a scree of mossy limestone blocks where cold air seeps out between the stones, and at the bottom, where the slope meets the coulee floor, is the Cold Hole: a low, wide cave mouth, its lip furred with frost on the hottest day of August, that breathes out, slowly, and in, slowly, like a sleeper. Nobody goes down there. Nobody needs to be told not to.

regions.name: Over the Water and Over the Ridge
regions.description: Hollow Fork's land ends where its water does: the watershed ridge that the county road climbs to the east, and the two branches of the creek, which join below the Hollow and run west to the Mississippi. Over the ridge is Linden Falls, the county seat, eighteen miles: Sheriff Clifford Dahlquist's office, the courthouse and register of deeds, the Kinnick County Library with the Linden Falls Courier on microfilm back to 1889, and the federal farm offices (the county ASCS office and the Soil Conservation Service) with their aerial photographs and watershed maps. West is La Crosse, the TV station, the Greyhound depot. Across the Mississippi, in Winona, Minnesota, lives Einar Aldahl, seventy-nine, of the family that left. The State Historical Society in Madison, three hours east, holds the Furrow's 1904 volume on microfilm, because the co-op sent copies of every issue to the Society's newspaper collection and forgot it had.

campaignRules.name: The Harvest Days Clock
campaignRules.description: The campaign runs on a calendar, twenty-two days from the party's arrival on Saturday 21 September 1974 to last light on Saturday 12 October, and the town acts on it whether or not the players are watching. Track the date openly and say how many days are left to Harvest Days whenever the players ask. hs-scenario-001 is the welcome (21 to 29 September); hs-scenario-002 the town's books (30 September to 6 October); hs-scenario-003 the corn at night (7 to 9 October); hs-scenario-004 Harvest Days (11 and 12 October). If nobody interferes, this happens. ALREADY DONE: on Labor Day, Monday 2 September, the co-op board (the heads of the six houses still in Hollow Fork) met in the co-op office, and Harald Haugen wrote 'Dawn Petrakis, Rockford, Ill.' in the Book. On Friday 13 September Dawn moved from the motel to the Fossums' hired man's house to help Lillian Fossum with the harvest cooking, and Elsie Brandvold wrote 'checked out 9/13' in the motel register. THE TOWN: on the night of Monday 23 September the killing frost comes and stops at the ridge and the creek; on Tuesday 24 September the La Crosse TV van comes for 'the town the frost forgot' and is invited back for Harvest Days; on Thursday 26 September the board meets about the strangers and Harald pencils an alternate name under Dawn's (the outsider who has eaten most of the town's food, usually Russ Thorsen if he is played); on Sunday 29 September the Fall Supper at the Community Church; on Wednesday 2 October Sheriff Dahlquist comes out from Linden Falls, has pie and coffee, tells the party there is no case, and goes home; on Monday 7 October Dawn is moved to Ingeborg Vaage's stone house at the Hollow's rim if the town knows the party has found her, and Arnie Fossum begins organising the men of the town on channel 14; on Tuesday 8 October the Fork bridge is closed 'for repairs' with two grain trucks and the county road over the ridge is blocked 'by a washout'; on Wednesday 9 October, if the party has tried to take Dawn, the town's line walks the Fossum corn that night; on Thursday 10 October the telephone exchange 'goes down'. HARVEST DAYS: Friday 11 October, the parade and the Harvest Queen (a grandmother, by tradition), the co-op open house; Saturday 12 October, the tractor pull at ten, the pie auction at two, the TV van live at six from the fairgrounds, the supper in the pavilion at five, and at last light, 6:21 p.m., the guest is walked to the Hollow rim 'to see the sunset' and goes down. If the rent is not paid by last light, see the Landlord's Rules.

campaignRules.name: The Landlord's Rules
campaignRules.description: GM ONLY until the players learn each one; never change a rule once learned. The Landlord is the thing in the Hollow, and it follows four rules, each with at least three clues (controlFile.clues). RULE ONE, THE GUEST: it may take only a guest, someone born outside the land that drains into the Hollow who has eaten bread made from Hollow Fork grain at a Hollow Fork table, and only the guest whose name is written in the Book before Harvest Days; only the hand that wrote a name can strike it out. A guest who eats at a Hollow Fork table day after day grows content and slow to leave (each day after the first that an outsider eats the town's food, a WIS save DC 10, +1 per day, or they feel the pull: disadvantage on checks to argue for leaving or to refuse hospitality that day; it is a feeling the GM describes, never a command). RULE TWO, THE BOUNDS: it cannot cross running water, and it cannot go beyond the land that drains into the Hollow: the watershed ridge and the two branches of the creek are its walls, and a hose left running across a doorstep is a wall too. RULE THREE, THE BREATH: it is blind; it finds the living by the warmth of their breath. Anyone who hides their breath, face down in the earth, or breathing through a cloth soaked in running water, or holding it as it passes, is passed by (advantage on Stealth against it; a held breath lasts one round per point of CON modifier, minimum one). Fire hurts it, and fire's warmth draws it. Its cold can hurt anyone who stands in its way; only a written guest can be taken. RULE FOUR, THE LEASE: the bargain is a lease and ends only two ways. It is surrendered when a living member of each of the seven houses that signed it (Haugen, Vaage, Brandvold, Kubicek, Lunde, Fossum, Aldahl; by blood or by marriage) reads their house's line from the Book's first page aloud at the Cold Hole at last light on Harvest Days. Or it is paid out when the hand that writes the names goes down into the Hollow in the guest's place. If a year's rent goes unpaid without either, the frost comes to Hollow Fork that night, and the Landlord walks its land until dawn hunting any outsider who has eaten the bread, and the next year two names are owed.

campaignRules.name: Dread in Hollow Fork
campaignRules.description: Use dread.json. Fear checks (WIS saves) in this campaign: DC 10 for a sign (frost on the inside of a window, a hose running in the dark, the motel register, a red kerchief left on a fence post, a voice in the corn); DC 15 for seeing it (the cold coming up the street as a ground fog that moves against the wind, the frost shape in the rows, the Cold Hole breathing in); DC 20 for the truth (the co-op's back room with seventy years of guests' suitcases; the Book's list of names; the guest walking down into the Hollow). Knowing one of the Landlord's rules lowers the DC by 2. Darkness adds 2. The same horror costs Dread once per scene. Recovery as dread.json: a lit, warm room with company, a long night's sleep, a drink, a cigarette, a laugh, a prayer. Note the trap: the warm room with company and the hot meal are, in Hollow Fork, the town's own; a short rest at the diner works, and costs a meal of the town's bread (Rule One). Once per scenario the light goes out at the worst moment. Table safety: ask at the start what the players do not want in the game, and honour 'skip that' at once.

campaignRules.name: The Good Neighbors
campaignRules.description: The town has one attitude toward the party, tracked by the GM and shown in how people behave rather than announced: WELCOMING (free rooms, pie, invitations, everyone's first name), CONCERNED (the same, with somebody always nearby: an offer of a ride, a job, a fixed fuel pump, a friendly question about plans), WATCHFUL (the CB talks about them, the phone line clicks, the motel has 'a plumbing problem' and moves them, nobody will drive them anywhere), and CLOSED (the bridge, the road, the phones, the Greyhound stop cancelled; a polite line of men in the dark). It starts at Welcoming. It moves toward Closed for asking about 1904, the Book, the suitcases or the Hollow in the wrong company, being seen at the Old Union Church or the co-op at night, talking to Dawn, talking to the sheriff or the TV crew about the town. It never moves back once Watchful. Individual keepers have their own attitudes (see controlFile.suspects) and can be turned. The town does not want to hurt anyone. It wants the rent paid and the strangers to go home; at Closed it will tackle, hold, lock in a root cellar and take car keys, but it does not shoot to kill, and a party that kills a townsman has made something worse of Hollow Fork than the Landlord ever did.

explorationRules: This is a small-town sandbox on a clock, and the map is a schematic of it: the village on its ridge spur in the middle, the co-op and the fairgrounds along the north branch of the creek, the Fossum place and its corn to the south, the Hollow below them, Linden Falls over the watershed ridge to the east, and La Crosse, the Mississippi and Winona far to the west. The party moves by car, pickup, eighteen-wheeler, the Greyhound (Tuesdays and Fridays, 4:10 p.m. westbound, 11:40 a.m. eastbound) or on foot; inside Hollow Fork everything is ten minutes away, Linden Falls is half an hour, La Crosse an hour, Winona an hour and a half, Madison three hours. The unit of time is the half-day, and the Harvest Days Clock (campaignRules) is the engine: every half-day spent in Madison is a half-day the town spends watching the party's motel rooms. Each scenario lists its places and who is in them. Run Hollow Fork as a real town with a real routine: milking at five and five, the co-op store open eight to six, the diner six to eight, church on Sunday, the Ridge Inn's Friday fish fry, the grain dryers running all night, and the CB always on. The investigation follows the three-clue rule (dread.json investigation, and the Landlord's Rules): core clues are found by anyone who looks in the right place; rolls add detail and speed, never dead ends. Fights are rare, short and frightening; most scenes are a kitchen table, a diner booth or a church basement with someone who is lying to the party out of kindness. Money is 1974 dollars: a cup of coffee is 25 cents, pie 50, a night in a motel $12 (free here), a gallon of gas 55 cents, a Polaroid SX-70 pack of ten pictures $6.50, a CB radio $130, a farm hand earns $3 an hour, an acre of good Wisconsin farmland sells for $600 and is about to sell for $900, and the co-op owes a Madison bank $1.2 million for its new grain dryer.

controlFile.note: The fixed truth of the campaign, for the GM only. It does not change because a player has a more exciting theory, and the Landlord's rules never change once learned. Hollow Fork, Kinnick County, Linden Falls, the Hollow Fork Farmers' Cooperative, the Hollow Fork State Bank, the Furrow, the Linden Falls Courier, the La Crosse TV station and every person in the campaign are fictional. The Driftless Area, its cold-air slopes, Wisconsin's dairy and grain economy, the 1970s grain boom and farm-credit boom that came before the farm crisis of the 1980s, CB radio, the Greyhound, Polaroid cameras and the State Historical Society's newspaper collection in Madison are real. The Landlord belongs to no religion, people or tradition; it was there before anyone, it has no worship and no name, and the town's churches have nothing to do with it (the one minister who knew, in 1904, refused it and wrote it down).
controlFile.theTruth: In the summer of 1904 Hollow Fork was dying. The 1903 hail had taken the wheat; the Bank of La Crosse had failed with the township's savings in it; the Northwestern Farm Mortgage Company of Milwaukee had foreclosed on eleven farms and was about to foreclose on twenty more; and a fever that August killed the township's doctor and five farmers and had Halvor Vaage's wife in bed and not expected to live. The families had always known the Hollow was odd: cold air in July, ice in the cave, cattle that would not graze the rim, a feeling. Halvor Vaage, sitting up with his wife, went down to the Cold Hole one night in despair and anger to see what was there, and something in the cold spoke to him, and offered terms. On the night of 24 August 1904 the heads of the seven families who had founded the co-op the year before (Halvor Vaage, Gunnar Haugen, Ole Brandvold, Josef Kubicek, Anders Lunde, Per Fossum, Knut Aldahl's father Tor Aldahl) went down together, heard the terms, and agreed. Gunnar Haugen, the co-op secretary, wrote the terms on the first page of the back half of the co-op's minute ledger, and all seven signed. Halvor told the township's minister, Rev. Caspar Penrose of the Union Church, and asked him to bless the first Harvest Supper; Penrose refused, wrote the whole thing down in the church register, preached one sermon against 'the bargain at the Hollow' to an empty church, hid the register under the pulpit floor and left in the spring of 1905; the Union Church closed and the town built the Community Church in the village in 1906. The first rent was Emmett Tilley, a seed salesman from Rockford, Illinois, the guest of honour at the first Harvest Supper on Saturday 15 October 1904, whom the Furrow reported 'departed on the evening stage'. Mrs. Vaage got up out of bed the next morning and lived to be ninety. The mortgage company's foreclosures were withdrawn that winter when the company itself failed. The hail has turned at the watershed ridge ever since. Since 1904 the Book has recorded seventy rents. In 1951 the rent went unpaid: Knut Aldahl, Tor's son and the Aldahl head of house, and his son Einar drove the guest, an encyclopedia salesman named Stanley Wachowski, over the Fork bridge in the night, and the frost followed them to the water and stopped. That night the frost killed Hollow Fork's corn for the only time in seventy years, and all that winter the Landlord walked the land at night, and the town drove the Aldahls out; in 1952 two names were written. Since 1955 the names have been written by Harald Haugen, Gunnar's grandson and the co-op's manager. The guest is chosen by the co-op board, the heads of the six houses still in town, at their Labor Day meeting: deliberately, in committee, someone passing through who has eaten the town's bread and who seems to have nobody. The town keeps the guest comfortable and content (the bread does most of it) until Harvest Days; the guest's car is driven to the Greyhound depot in La Crosse and left; the guest's luggage goes into the back room of the co-op, where it has gone for seventy years. The 1973 rent was Dr. Howard Gessler of Evanston, Illinois, a bowhunter whose guide, Russ Thorsen, has been coming back every month since. The 1974 rent is Dawn Petrakis of Rockford, who told Elsie Brandvold she had no family; she has a sister, Tess, who did not answer the phone the night Dawn called collect, and who has felt sick about it ever since. Dawn is alive, in the Fossums' hired man's house, being fed, cared for and kept, sleepy and content, by Lillian Fossum, who is kind to her and terrified. The 1974 season is the town's seventieth, and the hardest: the co-op owes $1.2 million on its new elevator and dryer, the State Bank holds $3.1 million in farm notes written in the land boom, Arnie Fossum bought four hundred acres in 1973 on credit, and every keeper knows what happens to towns whose luck runs out, because they can see it from the ridge.
suspects: Harald Haugen, 58, manager of the Hollow Fork Farmers' Cooperative and keeper of the Book: THE HAND THAT WRITES THE NAMES. Reason: his grandfather wrote the terms; he has written nineteen names since 1955, and he believes, with evidence from every town he can see from the ridge, that without the bargain the co-op fails, the bank fails and two hundred and twenty families lose their farms; the co-op's $1.2 million loan is his signature. He hates every name and has never missed one. Turnable: by his son Rolf, by the Book read back to him, by the faces of the guests in the back room. If the surrender fails, he may choose to pay the lease out himself (Rule Four). THIS IS WHAT SUCCEEDS IF NOBODY INTERFERES: Dawn goes down at last light on 12 October.

Marit Lunde, 54, president of the Hollow Fork State Bank: the hardest keeper. Reason: the bank holds $3.1 million in farm notes, a hundred and forty families' homes, many written in the 1973 to 1974 land boom on values that will not last without the luck. 'I have a hundred and forty families in that vault. You want me to trade them for one girl from Rockford.' She invited the TV station to film Harvest Days to bring in investors, and regrets it.

Arnie Fossum, 49, village president, the biggest farmer in Hollow Fork: the muscle. Reason: four hundred acres bought in 1973 at $600 an acre on credit, a new free-stall barn, three sons, and his grandfather's name in the Book. He runs the town's line in the corn on channel 14 and the roadblocks; he thinks he is protecting his town and will not hurt anyone if he can help it. His wife Lillian is keeping Dawn.

Dr. Arlen Kubicek, 66, the town doctor: the saved child's father. Reason: his son Gary had leukemia in 1958, at ten, and went into a remission no medicine of the time could explain; Gary is twenty-six now, the town's veterinarian, with a wife and two little girls. Arlen keeps the guests 'resting' and has signed every guest's 'fit to travel' note for thirty years. He knows exactly what he is, and he would do it again for Gary.

Elsie Brandvold, 61, the Fork Diner: the bread. Reason: her husband Arvid had a heart attack in 1959 that Dr. Kubicek said he would not survive, and he is out in the diner's kitchen every morning still; she is kind to everyone because she is kind, and she bakes the Harvest Supper bread from co-op flour because her mother did. She tells herself the guests go somewhere peaceful. She wrote 'checked out' in the motel register for twenty years.

Ingeborg Vaage, 82, the last witness: she was twelve in 1904 and watched her father go down into the Hollow so her mother would live. Reason: her mother did live, and so did the town; she has spent seventy years tending the guests' graves that are not graves and keeping the memory that nobody else will. She is the one keeper who wants it ended, and who will speak first at the Cold Hole if anyone asks her.
redHerrings: The Community Church and Pastor Tove Hagstrom. A new pastor, a church built in 1906, a town where everyone goes on Sunday: the players will suspect the church. They are wrong. The church has nothing to do with the bargain; Pastor Tove, who came in June, is an outsider, has been eating the town's bread for four months, and is as much in danger as the party. She is a companion, not a suspect.

Sheriff Clifford Dahlquist of Kinnick County. He is not in on it. He is tired, underfunded and lives over the ridge, and every missing-person report from Hollow Fork in twenty years has come with a motel register saying 'checked out' and a car found at the La Crosse bus depot. He has filed them all as adults who left of their own accord, which is what the evidence says. He can be convinced by the suitcases, the Book or a body of evidence; he cannot be convinced by talk of the Hollow.

The farm dogs, the crows on the Hollow rim, and the town's 'Gleaners' (the old name for the men's harvest crew). The dogs are dogs, the crows are crows and the Gleaners are farmers; none of them is the Landlord's creature, though all of them are part of its season.

A killer on the highway. Quentin Talbert's editor, the TV reporter Bonnie Sedlak and half the truckers on channel 19 have wondered about a man who picks up hitchhikers on the La Crosse road, and the CB has a name for him. There is no such man. The pattern is in Hollow Fork, not on the road, and the truth is stranger and plainer than any rumour: a lease, written in a co-op ledger by farmers in 1904, with something that belongs to nobody's tradition and no people's story.
clues: A. TRAVELERS VANISH FROM HOLLOW FORK EVERY HARVEST. A1: Quentin Talbert's list of eleven missing-persons reports in twenty years last placed in Kinnick County in September or October (hs-scenario-001). A2: the Harvest Moon Motel register: every September one guest 'checked out' in the same hand, Elsie's (hs-scenario-001). A3: Russ Thorsen's client, Dr. Gessler, in October 1973, and his car found at the La Crosse bus depot (hs-scenario-001). A4: the co-op's back room, seventy years of suitcases (hs-scenario-002). A5: the Book's list of names (hs-scenario-002).

B. DAWN NEVER LEFT. B1: her postcard to Tess postmarked Hollow Fork 16 September, three days after she 'caught the Friday bus' (hs-scenario-001). B2: the Greyhound driver, Emil Pospisil: no young woman got on at Hollow Fork on the 13th, and she gave him a peach at the diner counter on Tuesday the 10th (hs-scenario-001). B3: Lillian Fossum buying Dawn's brand of cigarettes, Kools, at the co-op store, though nobody at the Fossums' smokes (hs-scenario-001). B4: Ward Mrozek hears 'how's our guest, eating good?' on channel 14 (hs-scenario-001). B5: Dawn's Polaroids, in her knapsack in the co-op back room, the last of them dated in her hand 20 September at the Fossums' (hs-scenario-002).

RULE ONE, THE GUEST. 1a: the Book's list: every name is from out of town, and every entry notes the date the guest 'took supper' (hs-scenario-002). 1b: the Furrow, October 1904: 'by resolution of the Cooperative Board, every traveler is welcome at the Harvest Supper table, without charge' and Tilley 'departed on the evening stage', against the Linden Falls Courier's 'ROCKFORD MAN MISSING' (hs-scenario-002). 1c: Einar Aldahl: 'If you've eaten their bread you're a guest. If your name's in the Book you're the guest' (hs-scenario-002). 1d: Rev. Penrose's register: 'a stranger who has eaten of their bread and whose name is written' (hs-scenario-002). 1e: the pull itself, felt by any character who keeps eating at Elsie's (hs-scenario-001).

RULE TWO, THE BOUNDS. 2a: the frost of 23 September stops exactly at the ridge road and the creek banks, a line you can walk (hs-scenario-001). 2b: the ASCS office's watershed map in Linden Falls lies exactly over the hail-insurance adjuster's seventy-year hail line (hs-scenario-002). 2c: the hoses running across Hollow Fork's back steps on harvest nights, and Einar Aldahl's hose across his trailer step in Winona (hs-scenario-001 and 002). 2d: the Book's 1951 entry, 'UNPAID — went over the water', and Einar's story of the Fork bridge (hs-scenario-002).

RULE THREE, THE BREATH. 3a: frost forming on the inside of the motel window in the shape of the sleeper's breath, and only where they breathed (hs-scenario-001). 3b: Rev. Penrose's register: 'Kari Brandvold lay down in the furrow with her face in the earth when it came up the field, and it passed her by' (hs-scenario-002). 3c: the red harvest kerchiefs, worn at the throat in harvest season and pulled up over the mouth at night, soaked at the pump first, 'so it doesn't take you for a stranger' (hs-scenario-001). 3d: Ingeborg Vaage: 'It can't see, child. It listens for your breath' (hs-scenario-002 or 003). 3e: the Thin Place, for a Sensitive at the Cold Hole: the sense of something enormous tasting the air (any).

RULE FOUR, THE LEASE. 4a: the Book's first page: the terms of 24 August 1904, in Gunnar Haugen's hand, with seven signatures (hs-scenario-002). 4b: Rev. Penrose's register: 'It is a lease and they spoke it as a lease, to be surrendered by every house that signed it, at the place it was made, or paid out by the hand that writes the names going down in the guest's stead' (hs-scenario-002). 4c: Einar Aldahl: 'Father said there were two doors out, and they both cost' (hs-scenario-002). 4d: Ingeborg Vaage, who was there (hs-scenario-003). 4e: Signe Aldahl's photograph of the seven men at the Hollow rim, 1904, names on the back, in Sylvie Aldahl's handbag (hs-scenario-001).

theLandlord.name: The Landlord (the thing in the Hollow)
theLandlord.basis: A unique campaign creature. Where a number is needed, use the Bound Spirit (dread.json, adversaries.json) with these changes, and remember that it is less a monster to fight than a hazard with rules.
theLandlord.appearance: Never a body. Cold air that moves against the wind; a ground fog that comes up out of the Hollow and along a street or a corn row at walking pace; frost forming on everything it passes, glass, husks, hair, eyelashes; a long, slow inhalation, close by, like something tasting the air; in the corn, a tall shape that is only the place where the frost is thickest. When it speaks, it is in a voice made of cold, using the words of the last person who spoke to it, and the voices of guests it has taken.
theLandlord.statistics: AC 13; 110 hit points (it cannot be destroyed by damage: at 0 it sinks back into the earth and cannot rise again until the next night); speed 30 ft, through gaps and between stalks as easily as air. Resistant to bludgeoning, piercing and slashing from ordinary weapons (a shotgun blast scatters the fog for a moment and does half damage); immune to cold; vulnerable to fire (double damage, and fire drives it back 10 ft for a round, but fire's warmth also draws it to the one who holds it) and to running water (it cannot cross it at all; a hose played across its path is a wall for as long as the water runs, and a bucket of water that was running a minute ago, thrown into it, does 2d6 and drives it back 10 ft). Senses: it is blind; it perceives warm breath within 60 ft as a bat hears, and nothing else. Frost Touch: +6 to hit, reach 5 ft, 3d8 cold damage, and the target makes a CON save DC 14 or is restrained by numbing cold until the end of its next turn. The Long Breath (recharge 5-6): it breathes in; every creature within 20 ft who is breathing makes a CON save DC 14, taking 4d8 cold damage on a failure, half on a success; anyone hiding their breath is unaffected. Calling the Guest: a written guest who has eaten the bread and is within 30 ft at last light on Harvest Days walks toward it unless restrained, a WIS save DC 15 each round to stop for a round; a friend holding them, or speaking their real name and the name of their home, gives advantage. Fear: seeing it, DC 15; the truth of it, DC 20.
rules: It may take only a guest: born outside its land, fed on Hollow Fork bread, and written in the Book; only the hand that wrote a name can strike it.
It cannot cross running water or leave the land that drains into the Hollow.
It is blind and finds the living by their breath; a hidden breath is passed by.
The lease ends only when all seven houses surrender it at the Cold Hole, or when the hand that writes the names goes down in the guest's place.
theLandlord.wantsAndWhy: It wants what it has always had: one guest each harvest, and the warmth of the land. It does not hate the town; it keeps its side of the bargain exactly, and expects the same. It is patient, literal and very old, older than the ice, and it is not evil in any way it would understand. That is what makes it frightening.

controlFile.theKeyClue: Everything turns on the Book: the back half of the co-op's 1903 minute ledger, in the old Diebold safe in Harald Haugen's office. Its first page is the lease, and its seventy lines are the town's confession. Point every early clue at the co-op (Dawn's luggage is in its back room, the motel register was kept by a co-op board member's wife, the Furrow is the co-op's paper), and let Rolf Haugen, who has known the safe's combination since he was fourteen, be the door. If the party reaches hs-scenario-003 without the Book, Ingeborg Vaage sends for them and tells them what is in it from memory.
controlFile.outcomes: There is no clean ending, only costs. THE SURRENDER (the bargain broken): a living member of each of the seven houses reads their house's line from the Book at the Cold Hole at last light on 12 October. The Landlord fights it with cold and with offers (hs-scenario-004). If every speaker holds, the Cold Hole stops breathing for the first time in seventy years and the cold goes down into the earth for good. That night the frost the rest of the Midwest had three weeks earlier comes to Hollow Fork; the standing corn, half the town's harvest, dies in the field. Over the following years the luck is simply gone: the co-op cannot pay its loan and sells the elevator in 1976, the State Bank's notes go bad when the farm crisis comes, and some of the families the party came to like lose their farms like everyone else in the 1980s. The secret comes out (the suitcases, the Book), the sheriff and the state come, and the keepers face what the law makes of seventy years; whether anyone is ever charged is the GM's to decide, but nobody in Hollow Fork forgives the party. Nobody dies. Dawn goes home. THE PAYING OUT (the bargain paid): if the surrender fails or is never tried, Harald Haugen, the hand that writes the names, can strike Dawn's name and go down into the Hollow in her place at last light. It is his choice, made for his town and his son, never a player's to make for him; play it with gravity and fade out at the rim. The lease is paid out: the cold goes down for good, the harvest stands, the town keeps this one last good year and loses the luck from then on, and the secret can stay buried if the party lets it. A man the party may have come to like is gone, and Rolf inherits a co-op and a silence. THE RENT PAID: if the party does nothing, fails, or simply takes Dawn and leaves, someone goes down: Dawn, or the pencilled alternate (very possibly a player character who has been eating Elsie's pie), or, if the party has got every outsider out of the watershed, nobody, and the rent goes unpaid: the frost comes, the Landlord walks the land all night hunting anyone who has eaten the bread, and in 1975 two names will be written. THE EPILOGUE: whatever happens, end on the first Sunday after, with the church bell, the dryers silent or roaring, and one image of what the town has become: green corn, or black.
